entities.summary:
ABN AMRO is a Dutch bank formed through the merger of Algemene Bank Nederland and Amsterdam-Rotterdam Bank in 1991, which became one of Europe's largest banks before being acquired and then broken apart in one of the most dramatic corporate collapses in European banking history. The 2007 ABN AMRO acquisition for €71 billion by a consortium of Royal Bank of Scotland, Fortis, and Santander was Europe's largest banking deal — and contributed to the collapse of two of the three acquiring banks during the 2008 financial crisis.

ABN AMRO's roots trace to the Netherlands Trading Society (1824) founded by King William I to revive Dutch commercial banking after the Napoleonic Wars. The bank financed Dutch colonial enterprises in the East Indies, the construction of Amsterdam's financial district, and major European infrastructure projects. Its 1991 merger created a bank with 3,000 branches in 60 countries.

The 2007 acquisition consortium — RBS paying for LaSalle (US operations), Fortis for Dutch operations, Santander for Brazilian operations — dismembered ABN AMRO at the peak of the credit bubble. When the financial crisis hit, RBS required the UK's largest bank bailout (£45.5 billion), and Fortis was nationalized by Belgium, Netherlands, and Luxembourg. The Dutch government purchased the Dutch ABN AMRO operations from Fortis in 2008 for €16.8 billion, reconstituting ABN AMRO as a nationalized Dutch bank. It was re-privatized in 2015.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: ABN AMRO's €71 billion acquisition consortium collapse — destroying two of three acquiring banks and requiring bailouts totaling €60+ billion — is the most expensive example of credit bubble M&A hubris in European banking history.
